Clarke-Carbon Formula: N = ln(1−P) / ln(1−f). Calculates number of clones needed for complete genome representation at probability P.
Screening Method: Colony/plaque hybridisation with labelled probe, immunological screening, or PCR is used to find the clone of interest from the library.
HGP Connection: YAC and BAC genomic libraries were central to the Human Genome Project (1990–2003). EST projects used cDNA libraries.
cDNA in Medicine: Human insulin cDNA (from pancreatic cDNA library) was expressed in E. coli to produce recombinant insulin — first recombinant therapeutic protein (1982).
Expression Advantage: cDNA can be directly expressed in prokaryotes (no introns to splice) — genomic library clones of eukaryotic genes cannot be directly expressed in E. coli.

sa.q: What is a DNA library? Distinguish between a genomic DNA library and a cDNA library.
sa.a: Define DNA library: a collection of cloned DNA fragments in vectors maintained in host cells; represents the genetic information of a source organism. Genomic library: source = total genomic DNA; contains coding + non-coding + introns; tissue-independent; large number of clones needed. cDNA library: source = mRNA (via reverse transcriptase → cDNA); contains only expressed, intron-free sequences; tissue-specific; smaller number of clones. Key difference: genomic library has all genetic information; cDNA library has only information from actively transcribed genes at a specific time/tissue. Practical difference: cDNA can be directly expressed in E. coli (no introns); genomic eukaryotic gene clones cannot.

sa.q: Describe the steps involved in the construction of a cDNA library. What is the role of reverse transcriptase?
sa.a: Step 1: Isolate poly-A mRNA from target tissue using oligo-dT cellulose affinity chromatography. Step 2: First-strand cDNA synthesis — oligo-dT primer anneals to poly-A tail; reverse transcriptase synthesises cDNA using mRNA as template → mRNA:cDNA hybrid. Step 3: Degrade mRNA using RNase H or NaOH → single-stranded cDNA remains. Step 4: Second-strand synthesis — DNA Polymerase I synthesises complementary strand → ds-cDNA. Step 5: Add restriction enzyme linkers/adaptors → ligate into vector (e.g., lambda gt11, pUC) → transform into E. coli. Role of RT: catalyses mRNA → cDNA (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase); reverses central dogma; derived from retroviruses; requires primer (oligo-dT or random hexamer).

sa.q: Explain the construction of a genomic DNA library. Why is partial digestion preferred over complete digestion?
sa.a: Steps: isolate total genomic DNA → partial restriction enzyme digestion → size selection → ligation into vector → transformation of E. coli → collection of clones = library. Partial vs complete digestion: complete digestion always cuts at the same sites, missing regions between rare restriction sites; partial digestion produces overlapping, random fragments that together cover all sequences. Overlapping inserts are needed for chromosome walking and physical mapping — complete digestion cannot provide this. Library size calculated using Clarke-Carbon formula: N = ln(1−P) / ln(1−f). Vectors used: cosmids for 35–45 kb inserts; YACs for megabase inserts; lambda phage for ~20 kb inserts.

sa.q: Why is a cDNA library preferred over a genomic library for expressing eukaryotic genes in bacteria?
sa.a: Eukaryotic genes contain introns (non-coding intervening sequences) that are removed by splicing in eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotes (bacteria) lack the splicing machinery (spliceosome) needed to remove introns from pre-mRNA. If a genomic eukaryotic gene (with introns) is expressed in E. coli, the introns will be read as coding sequence → non-functional or truncated protein. cDNA is derived from processed mRNA (introns already removed) → it represents only the coding sequence (exons) → can be directly and correctly translated in E. coli. Example: human insulin cDNA expressed in E. coli produces functional insulin; human insulin genomic clone would not.

sa.q: Write a note on the applications of DNA libraries in biotechnology and medicine.
sa.a: Human Genome Project: YAC and BAC genomic libraries provided overlapping clones for physical mapping and sequencing the 3.2 Gb human genome. Recombinant drug production: Human insulin, growth hormone, erythropoietin cloned from cDNA libraries and expressed in bacteria/yeast for therapeutic use. Gene discovery: cDNA libraries from diseased tissues (cancer, Alzheimer's) vs normal tissues identify differentially expressed genes — potential drug targets. EST (Expressed Sequence Tag) projects: Partial sequencing of cDNA library clones generated millions of short gene markers cataloguing the human transcriptome. Chromosome walking: Genomic libraries used to navigate chromosomal regions to isolate disease genes (e.g., cystic fibrosis gene isolated by chromosome walking in 1989). Phage display: cDNA libraries cloned into phage display vectors to identify protein–protein interactions and novel antibodies.

gl.d: A collection of cloned DNA fragments (in vectors, inside host cells) that together represent the genetic information of a source organism. Exists as genomic library (total DNA) or cDNA library (expressed sequences).

The complete DNA content of an organism's cell, including all chromosomes with coding genes, introns, promoters, enhancers, repetitive sequences, and intergenic DNA. Present in all nucleated cells of the organism.

A DNA copy of an mRNA molecule, synthesised by reverse transcriptase. Contains only the coding (exon) sequences of a gene — no introns. Used in cDNA libraries and for expression of eukaryotic genes in prokaryotes.

An RNA-dependent DNA polymerase found in retroviruses (e.g., HIV, MMLV). Synthesises a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand from an mRNA template. Essential enzyme for cDNA synthesis and cDNA library construction.

A DNA molecule (plasmid, bacteriophage, cosmid, or YAC) used to carry a foreign DNA fragment into a host cell where it can replicate. Must have an origin of replication, selectable marker, and restriction sites for cloning.

The uptake of foreign DNA by a bacterial cell. In library construction, recombinant vectors are introduced into competent E. coli by transformation. Successfully transformed cells are selected on antibiotic plates.
The process of inserting a DNA fragment into a vector and propagating it in host cells to produce many identical copies of the fragment. Forms the basis of DNA library construction.
An enzyme that recognises and cuts double-stranded DNA at specific palindromic sequences. Used in genomic library construction to fragment total DNA into cloneable pieces with compatible ends.

A stretch of ~150–250 adenosine residues added to the 3' end of eukaryotic mRNA after transcription. Used to selectively purify mRNA from total RNA using oligo-dT cellulose chromatography during cDNA library preparation.

An enzyme that degrades the RNA strand of an RNA:DNA hybrid duplex. Used in cDNA synthesis to remove the mRNA template after first-strand cDNA synthesis, leaving single-stranded cDNA for second-strand synthesis.

A short partial sequence (300–500 bp) of a randomly selected cDNA clone. Used to identify genes without full sequencing. Millions of human ESTs generated from cDNA libraries helped catalogue the human transcriptome.

A technique for navigating across a chromosomal region using overlapping genomic library clones. Each new clone is used as a probe to identify the next overlapping clone, progressively moving along the chromosome toward a target gene.

gel_electrophoresis.html.title: Gel Electrophoresis
kp: Definition: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA/RNA/proteins based on size and charge using an electric field through a porous gel matrix acting as a molecular sieve.
DNA Charge: DNA is negatively charged (phosphate backbone). Migrates towards anode (+). Wells are ALWAYS at the cathode (−) end of the gel.
Migration Rule: Smaller fragments travel FASTER and FARTHER from wells. Larger fragments travel SLOWER and stay CLOSER to wells. log(bp) ∝ −distance.
Agarose Concentration: 0.5–0.8%: large DNA (2–50 kb). 1%: general use. 2–3%: small fragments (50–500 bp). Higher % = smaller pores = better resolution of small fragments.
PAGE: Polyacrylamide gel. Higher resolution than agarose. Can resolve single bp differences (DNA sequencing gels). Used for proteins and small DNA. Vertical orientation. Acrylamide is neurotoxic.
SDS-PAGE: SDS coats proteins with uniform negative charge proportional to molecular weight → separation by MW only. Used for protein characterisation and Western blotting.
DNA Ladder: Known-size fragment mixture run in lane 1. Allows construction of log(bp) vs distance standard curve. Unknown fragment sizes estimated by interpolation from this line.
Loading Dye: Glycerol increases density (sample sinks into well). Bromophenol blue (~300 bp) and xylene cyanol (~4 kb) track migration progress without UV.
EtBr: Intercalates into DNA; fluoresces orange under UV (302 nm). MUTAGENIC — safer alternatives SYBR Green, GelRed. Added to gel during casting or by post-run soaking.
Procedure Order: Prepare gel → load samples + ladder → apply 70–120 V → run 30–60 min → UV visualise → photograph → interpret against ladder.
Applications: PCR product verification, restriction mapping, DNA fingerprinting (forensics), clone confirmation, mutation detection, protein analysis (SDS-PAGE).
Common Errors: Smearing = DNase degradation or overload. No bands = failed PCR. Extra bands = non-specific amplification. Smile effect = overheating → reduce voltage.

sa.q: What is gel electrophoresis? Explain its principle with reference to DNA separation.
sa.a: Definition: technique to separate DNA/RNA/proteins based on size and charge using an electric field through a gel matrix acting as a molecular sieve. DNA is negatively charged (phosphate backbone) → migrates towards anode (+) when electric field applied. Gel = molecular sieve; smaller fragments navigate pores more easily → migrate farther; larger fragments retarded → stay closer to well. All DNA has same charge-to-mass ratio → separation is purely by SIZE via molecular sieving, not charge. Relationship: log(fragment size in bp) is inversely proportional to migration distance → straight line on semi-log graph. Include diagram: cathode (−), wells, gel slab, sample bands, DNA migration arrow, anode (+).

sa.q: Describe the procedure for agarose gel electrophoresis. List all components and their functions.
sa.a: Components and functions: Agarose (molecular sieve matrix); TAE buffer (pH maintenance, ionic conductivity, DNase inhibitor via EDTA); DNA sample; loading dye (glycerol = density, tracking dyes = migration monitor); DNA ladder (size standard); power supply (70–120 V DC); EtBr/SYBR Green (visualisation); UV transilluminator (band detection). Procedure (6 steps): (1) Prepare agarose gel in TAE → cool → add EtBr → pour with comb → solidify. (2) Place gel in buffer-filled chamber. (3) Mix samples with loading dye; load ladder + samples. (4) Apply 70–120 V; run 30–60 min until dye front 80% of gel. (5) Visualise under UV. (6) Photograph and interpret against ladder. Loading dye detail: glycerol prevents sample floating out of well; bromophenol blue provides visible tracking at ~300 bp equivalent position.

sa.q: Explain the relationship between DNA fragment size and migration distance. How is fragment size estimated from a gel?
sa.a: Inverse logarithmic relationship: log(fragment size in bp) is proportional to the negative of migration distance from well. Smaller bp → greater distance from well. Larger bp → smaller distance from well. On a semi-log plot (y = log bp, x = migration distance), ladder band positions form a STRAIGHT LINE. Size estimation method: (1) Measure migration distances of all ladder bands. (2) Plot log(bp) vs distance → draw best-fit straight line. (3) Measure migration distance of unknown sample band. (4) Read off corresponding log(bp) from the line → calculate bp. Physical explanation: gel = molecular sieve; larger fragments must negotiate multiple pore interactions simultaneously → retarded; smaller fragments slip through easily.

sa.q: Compare agarose gel electrophoresis with SDS-PAGE. What are the applications of each?
sa.a: Agarose gel: Matrix = agarose (0.5–3%); horizontal; separates DNA and RNA by SIZE; stain = EtBr/SYBR Green (UV); applications = PCR analysis, restriction mapping, DNA fingerprinting, Southern blot, clone verification. SDS-PAGE: Matrix = polyacrylamide + SDS; vertical; separates proteins by MOLECULAR WEIGHT only; SDS coats protein with uniform negative charge proportional to chain length → removes native charge/shape differences; stain = Coomassie Blue / silver stain; applications = protein MW determination, Western blot, proteomic analysis, recombinant protein purity. Key difference: agarose for nucleic acids; SDS-PAGE for proteins. SDS eliminates native protein charge — MW is sole separating factor. Both use electric field; both separate by size (through different mechanisms). Draw a comparison table: Feature | Agarose | SDS-PAGE — matrix, molecule, separation basis, orientation, stain, application.

sa.q: What is a DNA ladder? Why is it essential in gel electrophoresis? Give an example of a commonly used ladder.
sa.a: A DNA ladder (molecular weight marker) is a premixed solution of DNA fragments of precisely known sizes loaded in a dedicated lane alongside experimental samples. Examples: 100 bp ladder (bands at 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000 bp); 1 kb ladder (0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 kb); HyperLadder (multiple ranges). Why essential: without a ladder, it is impossible to determine the size of unknown fragments from their position alone — only relative positions are visible. Use: (1) provides reference migration distances for known sizes; (2) allows construction of log(bp) vs distance standard curve; (3) unknown fragment sizes estimated by interpolation. Some ladders have one prominent bright band (e.g., 500 bp in the 100 bp ladder or 1 kb in the 1 kb ladder) with double the DNA loading for easy orientation.

gl.d: Movement of charged molecules through a medium under an electric field. Negatively charged DNA migrates towards the positive electrode (anode). The rate of migration depends on the molecule's size, charge, and the resistance of the medium.

A linear polysaccharide extracted from red algae, used as the gel matrix in DNA/RNA electrophoresis. Forms a porous network when solidified from hot solution. Pore size is controlled by agarose concentration.
The positive (+) electrode in an electrophoresis system. Negatively charged DNA migrates towards the anode. Located at the end of the gel farthest from the sample wells.
The negative (−) electrode. DNA sample wells are always at the cathode end — DNA is loaded here and migrates away towards the anode when the electric field is applied.

A molecular weight standard containing a mixture of DNA fragments of precisely known sizes. Run alongside unknown samples in gel electrophoresis to provide a reference for size estimation by comparison of migration distances.

The porous network (agarose or polyacrylamide) through which molecules migrate in electrophoresis. Acts as a molecular sieve — resistance to migration increases with molecule size, enabling size-based separation.

Movement of DNA/RNA/protein through the gel under the applied electric field. Migration distance is inversely proportional to the log of fragment size: smaller fragments migrate farther than larger ones in the same time.

Process of making separated molecules visible after electrophoresis. For DNA: ethidium bromide (EtBr) intercalates into DNA and fluoresces under UV. Safer alternatives: SYBR Green, GelRed. For proteins: Coomassie Blue, silver stain.

Solution mixed with DNA before loading into wells. Contains glycerol or Ficoll (increases density, keeps sample in well) and tracking dyes (bromophenol blue ≈ 300 bp; xylene cyanol ≈ 4 kb) for visible monitoring of migration.

Fluorescent dye that intercalates between DNA base pairs. Fluoresces bright orange under UV light (302 nm), making DNA bands visible. Detects ~1–10 ng DNA per band. Potent mutagen and carcinogen — safer alternatives include SYBR Green and GelRed.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.title: Gene Cloning – Steps & Selection of Clones
kp: Gene Cloning: Process of making identical copies of a specific gene by inserting it into a vector, introducing into a host cell, and allowing replication. Core of recombinant DNA technology.
5 Requirements: Source DNA + Vector + Restriction enzyme + DNA ligase + Host cell (E. coli). Together they enable the entire cloning process.
Restriction Enzymes: Must use the same enzyme on insert and vector to produce compatible sticky ends. Common examples: EcoRI (GAATTC), BamHI (GGATCC), HindIII (AAGCTT).
DNA Ligase (T4): Seals phosphodiester bonds between 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate ends. Joins insert into vector. Requires ATP and Mg²⁺. Usually incubated at 16°C overnight.
Transformation: Introduction of recombinant DNA into E. coli. Methods: CaCl₂/heat shock (42°C) or electroporation. Only ~1 in 10³–10⁵ cells is transformed.
Antibiotic Selection: Cells plated on medium with ampicillin. Only cells carrying the vector (amp^r) survive. This selects for transformed cells (but not specifically recombinants).
Blue-White Screening: Blue colonies = non-recombinant (lacZ intact, β-gal active, cleaves X-gal → blue). White colonies = recombinant (insert disrupts lacZ, no β-gal, no colour). Pick WHITE colonies!
Insertional Inactivation: In pBR322: insert into BamHI/SalI site disrupts tet^r. Recombinants = amp^r, tet^s. Non-recombinants = amp^r, tet^r. Confirmed by replica plating.
Alkaline Phosphatase: Removes 5'-phosphates from linearised vector to prevent self-ligation. Dramatically reduces background of non-recombinant colonies.
Correct Cloning Sequence: Isolate gene → Restriction digest → Ligate → Transform → Select on antibiotic → Screen (blue/white or insertional inactivation) → Confirm → Amplify.
Colony Hybridisation: Probe-based screening to identify clone with specific gene. Colonies transferred to membrane → lysed → probed with labelled DNA → positive clones detected by autoradiography.
pUC19 vs pBR322: pUC19: uses lacZ/blue-white screening; MCS within lacZ. pBR322: uses insertional inactivation; two resistance genes (amp^r + tet^r); insert disrupts tet^r.

sa.q: Define gene cloning. Describe the step-by-step procedure of gene cloning.
sa.a: Definition: gene cloning = producing multiple identical copies of a specific gene using recombinant DNA technology. Steps in order: (1) Isolation of gene of interest (RE digestion/PCR/cDNA); (2) Restriction digestion of gene and vector with same RE; (3) Ligation with T4 DNA ligase; (4) Formation of recombinant DNA; (5) Transformation into E. coli (heat shock/electroporation); (6) Selection on antibiotic medium; (7) Screening for recombinants; (8) Colony multiplication and verification. Mention requirements: insert DNA, vector (ori + marker + MCS), restriction enzyme, DNA ligase, competent E. coli. Include a simple flow diagram: gene → RE cut → ligation → transform → select → screen.

sa.q: What is blue-white screening? Explain its principle and significance in clone selection.
sa.a: Blue-white screening uses the lacZ gene (encoding β-galactosidase) in pUC vectors to distinguish recombinant (white) from non-recombinant (blue) colonies. Principle: MCS is within lacZ. Without insert → lacZ intact → β-gal produced → cleaves X-gal → blue compound → blue colony. With insert → lacZ disrupted → no functional β-gal → X-gal not cleaved → white colony. Medium: LB agar + ampicillin (select transformants) + X-gal + IPTG (lac operon inducer). Significance: rapid visual screening without replica plating; picks white colonies as potential recombinants. Limitation: blue-white only shows insert disrupted lacZ — must confirm with PCR/restriction analysis.

sa.q: What is insertional inactivation? How is it used to select recombinant clones in pBR322 cloning?
sa.a: Insertional inactivation: inserting foreign DNA into a restriction site within a selectable marker gene disrupts that gene's function. pBR322 has two markers: amp^r (ampicillin resistance) and tet^r (tetracycline resistance) + unique restriction sites within each. Insert into BamHI or SalI (within tet^r): recombinants = amp^r, tet^s; non-recombinants = amp^r, tet^r. Protocol: grow all colonies on ampicillin → replica plate to tetracycline → colonies growing on amp but NOT tet = recombinants. Advantage: can identify recombinants with any insert (not dependent on lacZ); disadvantage: requires replica plating (more steps than blue-white).

sa.q: Explain the role of restriction enzymes and DNA ligase in gene cloning.
sa.a: Restriction enzymes ("molecular scissors"): recognise specific palindromic sequences; cleave both strands at/near the site; produce sticky (staggered cut) or blunt (straight cut) ends; Type II used in cloning (e.g., EcoRI, BamHI); same enzyme used on insert and vector ensures compatible ends. DNA ligase ("molecular glue"): T4 DNA ligase seals phosphodiester bonds; requires ATP and Mg²⁺; joins 3'-OH to 5'-phosphate; conditions: 16°C overnight for sticky ends; joins insert to vector to form recombinant DNA. Together: RE cuts open the vector at MCS and cuts the gene from the source genome with matching ends → ligase joins them to create a continuous circular recombinant DNA molecule.

sa.q: Why is selection necessary after transformation? Describe TWO methods of clone selection.
sa.a: Why selection: transformation is inefficient (~1 in 10³–10⁵ cells takes up vector); the ligation mixture contains non-recombinant (re-ligated) vectors AND recombinant vectors; all transformed cells look identical; selection is needed to identify cells carrying the correct recombinant vector. Method 1 — Antibiotic selection: vectors carry amp^r; transformed cells plated on ampicillin medium; only cells with vector survive; distinguishes transformed from non-transformed. Cannot distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant — further screening needed. Method 2 — Blue-white screening: pUC vectors; lacZ + MCS; X-gal + IPTG in medium; white colonies = recombinant (insert disrupts lacZ). Quick visual identification. Alternative Method 2 — Insertional inactivation: pBR322; insert disrupts tet^r; recombinants = amp^r + tet^s; detected by replica plating.

gl.d: The process of making multiple identical copies of a specific gene by inserting it into a vector, introducing the recombinant vector into a host cell, and propagating the host through cell division.

A DNA molecule (plasmid, phage, cosmid) used to carry a foreign gene into a host cell. Must have an origin of replication, selectable marker, and restriction sites. Acts as the "vehicle" for gene delivery.

The covalent joining of two DNA molecules by DNA ligase. Forms phosphodiester bonds between the 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate termini of compatible DNA ends. Creates the recombinant DNA molecule in gene cloning.
The uptake of foreign DNA by a bacterial cell. In gene cloning, competent E. coli cells take up recombinant vectors by heat shock (CaCl₂ method) or electroporation.

A hybrid DNA molecule formed by joining DNA sequences from two different sources — specifically the gene of interest (insert) ligated into a cloning vector. The central product of the cloning process.
A gene on the vector (usually an antibiotic resistance gene) used to identify and select transformed host cells. Only cells carrying the vector survive on medium with the corresponding antibiotic.

A method to distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant clones. White colonies carry an insert (lacZ disrupted, no β-gal, X-gal not cleaved). Blue colonies have no insert (lacZ intact, β-gal cleaves X-gal → blue colour).

Disruption of a marker gene (e.g., tet^r) by inserting foreign DNA into a restriction site within it. Cells with the insert lose function of that marker. Used to distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant clones.
A bacterial cell that has been chemically (CaCl₂) or physically (electroporation) treated to become capable of taking up exogenous DNA from its environment during transformation.

Short single-stranded complementary overhangs produced by staggered restriction enzyme cuts. Compatible sticky ends on the insert and vector anneal by hydrogen bonding, facilitating efficient ligation.

5-Bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-β-D-galactopyranoside — a synthetic colourless substrate for β-galactosidase. When cleaved by β-gal, it produces a blue compound. Used in blue-white screening with IPTG inducer.
A probe-based screening method. Bacterial colonies are lysed on a nylon membrane, DNA denatured, and a labelled probe applied. Hybridisation reveals which colony contains the target gene.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.title: Introduction of Recombinant DNA into Host Cells
kp: Transformation (Prokaryotes): CaCl₂ + heat shock (42°C) makes bacteria competent. DNA enters through temporary pores. Only for bacteria. Select transformants on antibiotic plates.
Transfection (Eukaryotes): Non-viral delivery of DNA into eukaryotic cells. Chemical (CaPO₄, cationic lipids) or physical (electroporation, microinjection). Transient or stable expression.

Transduction (Viral): Most efficient in vivo method. Modified virus delivers gene via receptor-mediated infection. Types: retrovirus (stable), lentivirus (non-dividing), adenovirus (episomal), AAV (safe, long-term).
Microinjection: Physical injection of DNA directly into nucleus using glass needle and micromanipulator. Primary method for transgenic mouse production. One cell at a time — low throughput.
Electroporation: High-voltage electric pulse creates temporary pores in lipid bilayer. DNA enters through pores. Universal — works for bacteria and eukaryotes. Best for hard-to-transfect cells.
Liposome Fusion: Cationic lipids form lipoplexes with DNA. Cell uptake via endocytosis + endosomal escape. Targetable. Basis of mRNA vaccines (LNPs) and siRNA therapeutics.

Key Distinction: Transformation = prokaryotes. Transfection = eukaryotes (non-viral). Transduction = viral. Microinjection = direct nuclear injection. Electroporation = electric pores. Liposome = lipid vesicle fusion.
Most Efficient In Vivo: Transduction (viral vectors) is most efficient for in vivo gene delivery, especially AAV and lentiviral vectors used in FDA-approved gene therapies.
Nuclear Barrier: Eukaryotic cells have a nuclear membrane — DNA must cross both plasma membrane AND nuclear envelope, unlike prokaryotes where only the plasma membrane must be crossed.
AAV Gene Therapies: Luxturna (RPE65 gene — blindness), Zolgensma (SMN1 gene — spinal muscular atrophy), Hemgenix (F9 gene — haemophilia B) — all use AAV vectors.
mRNA Vaccines: Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines use lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to deliver mRNA into muscle cells — a revolutionary application of liposome technology.

Stable vs Transient: Stable integration: retroviral, lentiviral, some transfection (permanent). Transient: adenoviral, plasmid transfection (temporary, no integration). Critical for choosing right method.

sa.q: What is transformation? Describe the steps involved in artificial transformation of E. coli.
sa.a: Definition: uptake of naked exogenous DNA by a bacterial cell leading to heritable change. First described by Griffith (1928); molecular basis by Avery et al. (1944). Steps: (1) Grow E. coli to log phase; (2) Wash in ice-cold CaCl₂ → competent cells; (3) Add recombinant plasmid DNA, incubate on ice (DNA adsorbs to cell surface); (4) Heat shock at 42°C for 90 sec → DNA enters through temporary membrane disruptions; (5) Recovery in LB medium at 37°C; (6) Plate on antibiotic selection medium → transformants survive. Transformation efficiency: 10⁵–10⁸ transformants/µg DNA. Alternative: electroporation gives 10–100× higher efficiency.

sa.q: Explain transduction as a method of gene transfer. What are the types of viral vectors used?
sa.a: Definition: gene delivery using modified viral vectors; most efficient method for in vivo delivery. Principle: viral pathogenic/replication genes removed → gene of interest inserted → packaged using packaging cell line → replication-deficient recombinant virus produced. Types: (a) Retrovirus (MLV) — stable integration, dividing cells only; (b) Lentivirus (HIV-derived) — stable, non-dividing cells, used in CAR-T; (c) Adenovirus — high efficiency, episomal, transient; (d) AAV — safe, long-term expression, used in Luxturna, Zolgensma. Limitations: insert size limited by capsid; insertional mutagenesis risk (retroviruses); immune response.

sa.q: Describe electroporation and liposome fusion as methods for introducing DNA into eukaryotic cells.
sa.a: Electroporation: high-voltage electric pulse (0.1–10 kV/cm) → temporary pores in lipid bilayer → DNA enters by electrophoresis and diffusion → pores reseal → cell recovers. Works for bacteria and eukaryotes. Good for hard-to-transfect cells. Used for CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. Liposome fusion: cationic lipids + DNA → lipoplex → binds cell surface (electrostatic) → endocytosis → endosomal escape → DNA in cytoplasm → nuclear entry. Advantages: protects DNA; targetable; in vivo use. Example: LNPs in mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. Compare: electroporation is physical (electric); liposome is chemical (lipid-based). Both can transfect non-dividing cells. Liposomes can be targeted; electroporation is universal.

sa.q: What is microinjection? Explain its role in creating transgenic animals.
sa.a: Definition: direct mechanical injection of DNA into individual cells using glass needle (0.1–0.5 µm tip) under micromanipulator guidance. Procedure: fertilised egg held by suction pipette → DNA solution in injection needle → needle inserted into male pronucleus → DNA injected → egg transferred to surrogate mother. Transgenic mouse creation: pioneer work by Gordon and Ruddle (1981). DNA integrates randomly into chromosomes → expression in all cells of resulting animal → stable germline transmission. Advantages: direct, no carrier needed; can deliver any molecule. Limitations: extremely low throughput (one cell at a time); high technical skill; cell damage risk. Clinical application: ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection) in human IVF.

sa.q: Compare any four methods of introducing recombinant DNA into host cells. (4-mark table question)
sa.a: (structured as a comparison table): Transformation: Prokaryotes; CaCl₂/heat shock; moderate efficiency; simple, cheap; bacteria only; gene cloning. Transduction: Eukaryotes (dividing + non-dividing); viral infection; very high efficiency; stable integration; capsid size limit; gene therapy. Electroporation: Prokaryotes + eukaryotes; electric pulse creates pores; high efficiency; universal; high cell death risk; CRISPR delivery. Microinjection: Large cells (oocytes); mechanical injection into nucleus; high per cell but very low throughput; direct, no carrier; transgenic animals. Liposome Fusion: Eukaryotes; lipoplex + endocytosis + endosomal escape; moderate–high; targetable; endosomal entrapment; mRNA vaccines, siRNA delivery. Draw a table with columns: Method | Cell Type | Mechanism | Efficiency | Application.

gl.d: The uptake of naked exogenous DNA by a bacterial cell, leading to a heritable change. In the laboratory, bacteria are made artificially competent using CaCl₂ and heat shock to take up plasmid DNA.

The introduction of foreign nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) into eukaryotic cells by non-viral methods. Includes chemical methods (calcium phosphate, cationic lipids) and physical methods (electroporation, microinjection). Can be transient or stable.

The delivery of foreign genetic material into host cells using a viral vector. The pathogenic genes of the virus are replaced by the gene of interest; the recombinant virus infects cells with high efficiency but cannot replicate.

A modified virus used as a gene delivery vehicle. The viral genes responsible for disease and replication are removed and replaced by the therapeutic gene. Common types include AAV, lentivirus, adenovirus, and retrovirus.

A physical method of gene delivery in which a brief high-voltage electric pulse (0.1–10 kV/cm) applied to cells in the presence of DNA creates temporary nanopores in the plasma membrane, through which DNA enters the cell.

A spherical artificial lipid bilayer vesicle that can encapsulate DNA, RNA, drugs, or other molecules. Cationic liposomes form complexes (lipoplexes) with negatively charged DNA for cellular delivery by membrane fusion or endocytosis.

A physical technique in which DNA or other molecules are directly injected into individual cells (usually into the nucleus or cytoplasm) using an ultra-fine glass capillary needle controlled by a micromanipulator under microscopic guidance.

A bacterial cell that is capable of taking up exogenous DNA. Natural competence occurs in some species; artificial competence is induced in E. coli by CaCl₂ treatment, making cells able to take up plasmid DNA during heat shock transformation.

An advanced, nanoscale lipid-based delivery vehicle (~80–150 nm) that encapsulates mRNA or siRNA, protecting it from nuclease degradation. LNPs were used in COVID-19 mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna) to deliver mRNA into human cells.

A transfection outcome in which the foreign DNA integrates into the host cell chromosome, becoming permanently heritable in all daughter cells. Required for long-term gene expression studies and therapeutic applications.

The process by which DNA, RNA, or other cargo delivered via endocytosis escapes from the endosome before lysosomal fusion and degradation. A critical step in efficient liposome-mediated and nanoparticle-based gene delivery.

A small, non-pathogenic, single-stranded DNA virus used as a gene therapy vector. Provides long-term gene expression with minimal immune response. Used in approved gene therapies: Luxturna (blindness), Zolgensma (SMA), Hemgenix (haemophilia).

molecular_markers_app.html.title: Molecular Markers: RFLP, RAPD & DNA Fingerprinting
kp: Molecular markers detect genetic variation (polymorphism) at the DNA level — unaffected by environment.
RFLP = Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism — restriction enzymes cut DNA → different individuals produce fragments of different lengths detected by Southern blotting.
RAPD = Random Amplified Polymorphic DNA — arbitrary short primers amplify multiple random loci by PCR — no sequence knowledge needed; dominant marker.
DNA fingerprinting exploits highly variable VNTR/STR regions — each individual has a unique number of repeats → unique band pattern (DNA profile).
RFLP is co-dominant (detects heterozygotes); RAPD is dominant (only presence/absence); DNA fingerprinting is co-dominant.
DNA fingerprinting was pioneered by Sir Alec Jeffreys (1984); first legal use in 1986.
Applications of DNA fingerprinting: forensics, paternity, criminal investigation, individual ID, wildlife conservation, population and biodiversity studies.
Molecular markers in biotechnology: genetic diversity, species ID, gene mapping, marker-assisted selection (MAS), evolutionary studies, medical diagnosis.
RAPD: fastest and cheapest; RFLP: most reliable; DNA fingerprinting: most discriminatory for individuals.
Modern forensic DNA profiling uses STR analysis at 15–20 loci — probability of a coincidental match is less than 1 in a trillion.

sa.q: What are molecular markers? Describe the principle and procedure of RFLP with a suitable diagram.
sa.a: Define molecular marker (specific DNA sequence detecting polymorphism). RFLP principle: restriction enzymes cut at recognition sites → mutations alter fragment lengths. Steps: DNA isolation → restriction digestion → gel electrophoresis → Southern blotting → probe hybridisation → band pattern analysis. Diagram: DNA → enzyme cuts → two different fragment sizes → gel bands. Mention co-dominant nature and applications (gene mapping, plant breeding).

sa.q: Explain the principle and steps involved in RAPD analysis. What are its advantages over RFLP?
sa.a: RAPD principle: single arbitrary ~10 nt primer binds at multiple sites at low annealing temperature → PCR amplifies random segments → presence/absence polymorphism. Steps: DNA isolation → PCR with random primer → gel electrophoresis → band pattern analysis. Advantages over RFLP: no prior sequence knowledge, smaller DNA quantity, no radioactive probes, faster, cheaper. Mention dominant marker limitation.

sa.q: Describe the principle of DNA fingerprinting and discuss its applications in forensic science and paternity testing.
sa.a: Principle: VNTRs/STRs are highly variable between individuals → different repeat numbers → unique fragment sizes → unique band profile (DNA fingerprint). Pioneer: Sir Alec Jeffreys, 1984. Steps: DNA isolation → PCR/RFLP of VNTR loci → gel separation → band profile → comparison. Forensics: crime scene DNA profile matched to suspect. Paternity: child inherits 50% from each parent — profile comparison confirms/excludes parentage.

sa.q: Compare RFLP, RAPD, and DNA Fingerprinting with reference to principle, technique, advantages, limitations, and applications.
sa.a: Use a table format. RFLP: restriction enzyme, Southern blot, co-dominant, high reproducibility, expensive, used in gene mapping. RAPD: PCR with random primer, dominant, low reproducibility, cheap, used for diversity studies. DNA FP: VNTR/STR variation, co-dominant, highly discriminatory, forensics/paternity. Distinguish co-dominant vs dominant. Mention sequence knowledge requirement: RFLP needs it; RAPD does not; DNA FP partially does.

sa.q: Discuss the role of molecular markers in biotechnology. Give examples of their importance in agriculture and medicine.
sa.a: Cover: genetic diversity assessment, species/strain identification, gene mapping, marker-assisted selection (MAS), evolutionary studies, medical diagnostics. Agriculture: crop improvement (disease resistance, yield), plant taxonomy, identification of plant pathogens. Medicine: diagnosis of genetic disorders, forensic identification, bone marrow transplant confirmation, infectious disease pathogen identification. Give 2–3 concrete examples for each domain.

gl.d: The existence of multiple genetically distinct forms at a locus within a population. Molecular markers detect and measure polymorphism.
An enzyme that cuts double-stranded DNA at specific short palindromic recognition sequences (restriction sites).
A short single-stranded DNA or RNA sequence (~10–25 nt) that provides a starting point for DNA synthesis in PCR.
The process of producing many copies of a specific DNA segment using PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction).
The arrangement of DNA fragments separated by gel electrophoresis, appearing as bands at positions corresponding to fragment size.
A specific DNA segment of known chromosomal location used to identify genetic variation between individuals or populations.
A set of DNA characteristics (band positions or allele sizes) that are unique to an individual and used for identification.
Variable Number Tandem Repeat — a region of the genome where a short sequence motif is repeated, with the repeat number varying between individuals.
Short Tandem Repeat — a short (2–6 bp) sequence repeated in tandem; highly variable and widely used in modern DNA fingerprinting.
A technique (developed by Edwin Southern) for transferring DNA fragments from a gel to a membrane for detection by probe hybridisation.
A marker that allows both alleles (e.g., AA, Aa, aa) to be distinguished — unlike dominant markers which only show presence or absence.
Using molecular markers linked to desirable genes to select individuals during breeding, without needing to wait for phenotype expression.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.title: PCR: Principle, Types & Applications
kp: PCR Full Form: Polymerase Chain Reaction. Invented by Kary Mullis in 1983. Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1993. In vitro DNA amplification technique.
Principle: Exponential amplification using thermal cycling: denaturation → annealing → extension. Produces 2ⁿ copies after n cycles. ~10⁹ copies after 30 cycles.
Taq Polymerase: From Thermus aquaticus. Heat-stable (survives 95°C). Optimal at 72°C. Rate ~1000 bp/min. Lacks proofreading (3'→5' exonuclease).
Three PCR Steps: Denaturation (94–96°C) → Annealing (50–65°C) → Extension (72°C). Each cycle doubles the DNA. 25–40 cycles typical.
Mg²⁺ Role: Essential cofactor for Taq polymerase. Also stabilises primer–template duplexes. Optimal: 1.5–2.5 mM. Excess Mg²⁺ causes non-specific amplification.
RT-PCR: RNA → cDNA (by reverse transcriptase) → PCR. Used for RNA virus detection. Basis of COVID-19 diagnostic test. Not the same as quantitative PCR (qPCR).
qPCR: Real-time monitoring of amplification using fluorescent dyes (SYBR Green) or probes (TaqMan). Quantitative. Used for viral load measurement and gene expression.
Multiplex PCR: Multiple primer pairs in one reaction. Amplifies several targets simultaneously. Used in forensic STR profiling and multi-pathogen panels.
Nested PCR: Two sequential PCRs. Outer primers first, then inner (nested) primers on the product. Highest sensitivity and specificity for low-copy targets.
Applications: Medical diagnosis (COVID, HIV), forensics (DNA fingerprinting), genetic disorders (cystic fibrosis), gene cloning, animal biotechnology, archaeological DNA.
Limitations: Prior sequence knowledge needed. Contamination causes false positives. Taq errors (no proofreading). Non-specific bands if Mg²⁺ or annealing T not optimised.
Primers: 18–25 nt synthetic oligos. Two required: forward + reverse. Complementary to template flanking the target. Annealing T = Tm − 5°C. Define the amplicon.

sa.q: What is PCR? Explain its principle and the three stages of a PCR cycle.
sa.a: Definition: Polymerase Chain Reaction — in vitro exponential amplification of a specific DNA segment using thermal cycling. Invented by Kary Mullis (1983); Nobel Prize 1993. Principle: repeated cycles of denaturation → annealing → extension; each cycle doubles copies; exponential amplification = 2ⁿ after n cycles. Stage 1 — Denaturation: 94–96°C; H-bonds broken; dsDNA → 2 ssDNA templates. Stage 2 — Annealing: 50–65°C; primers (forward + reverse) bind complementary template sequences; Tm−5°C rule. Stage 3 — Extension: 72°C; Taq polymerase adds dNTPs 5'→3' from primers; rate ~1000 bp/min. After 30–40 cycles → ~10⁶–10⁹ copies. Include a diagram of the temperature cycle.

sa.q: What are the components required for PCR? State the function of each.
sa.a: Template DNA — source DNA with target sequence. Primers (×2, forward + reverse) — define amplicon; 18–25 nt; provide 3'-OH for extension. Taq DNA polymerase — heat-stable; from T. aquaticus; synthesises new strand at 72°C. dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP) — building blocks for DNA synthesis. PCR buffer (Tris-HCl, KCl) — maintains optimal pH 8.3–8.8. MgCl₂ (1.5–2.5 mM) — essential polymerase cofactor; stabilises primer-template duplexes. Thermal cycler — automated temperature control. Exam tip: Know the role of Mg²⁺ separately — it's frequently asked alone.

sa.q: What is RT-PCR? How does it differ from conventional PCR and what are its applications?
sa.a: RT-PCR = Reverse Transcriptase PCR. Uses RNA as starting material, not DNA. Key step: RNA → cDNA by reverse transcriptase (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) BEFORE PCR. Two-step process: (1) RT step: mRNA + oligo-dT primer + RT enzyme → cDNA; (2) PCR: cDNA amplified by standard thermal cycling. Difference from conventional PCR: conventional uses DNA template directly; RT-PCR requires reverse transcription first to convert RNA to cDNA. Applications: detection of RNA viruses (SARS-CoV-2, HIV, influenza); gene expression analysis; transcriptome studies. COVID-19 diagnosis: RT-qPCR combines reverse transcription + real-time PCR.

sa.q: What is exponential amplification in PCR? Calculate the number of copies after 20 cycles.
sa.a: Exponential amplification: each cycle doubles the target DNA, so copies increase as powers of 2. Formula: Number of copies = 2ⁿ (where n = number of cycles starting from 1 molecule). After 20 cycles: 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 ≈ 1 million copies. After 30 cycles: 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 × 10⁹ ≈ 1 billion copies. Why exponential? Because products of each cycle serve as templates in the next cycle — not just the original two strands. Practical note: efficiency is not 100% in real reactions, so actual yield is somewhat lower (typically 80–90% efficiency per cycle).

sa.q: Describe the applications of PCR in medical diagnosis, forensics, and animal biotechnology.
sa.a: Medical diagnosis: RT-PCR detects RNA viruses (SARS-CoV-2 → COVID-19, HIV, hepatitis C); conventional PCR detects bacterial pathogens (M. tuberculosis, Chlamydia); multiplex PCR panels detect multiple pathogens in one test. Genetic disorder analysis: Detects mutations in CFTR (cystic fibrosis), HBB (sickle cell), BRCA1/2 (breast cancer); prenatal diagnosis from amniotic fluid cells. Forensic science: STR profiling by multiplex PCR from blood, hair, skin cells at crime scenes; DNA fingerprinting for identification; paternity testing. Animal biotechnology: Sex determination of embryos (SRY gene); detection of transgene integration in transgenic animals; breed/species identification; detection of animal pathogens; quality control of animal products. Gene cloning: Amplifies gene of interest for cloning into vector; colony PCR confirms successful insertion.

gl.d: An in vitro technique for amplifying a specific DNA segment exponentially using repeated thermal cycling steps (denaturation, annealing, extension) and a thermostable DNA polymerase. Invented by Kary Mullis in 1983.
The source DNA containing the target sequence to be amplified in PCR. Can be genomic DNA, cDNA, plasmid DNA, or forensic/clinical samples. Typically used in nanogram quantities per reaction.

A short (18–25 nt) synthetic single-stranded oligonucleotide complementary to the template flanking the target region. Two primers are required: forward (sense) and reverse (antisense). Defines the exact boundaries of the amplified product (amplicon).
The first stage of each PCR cycle. Heating to 94–96°C breaks hydrogen bonds between base pairs, separating the double-stranded DNA into single-stranded templates for primer binding in the next step.

The second stage of each PCR cycle (50–65°C). Primers hybridise to their complementary sequences on the single-stranded template through Watson-Crick base pairing. Annealing temperature = Tm − 5°C of the primers.
The third stage of each PCR cycle (72°C). Taq DNA polymerase extends each primer by adding dNTPs complementary to the template in the 5'→3' direction, synthesising a new complementary DNA strand.

A thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium from hot springs. Withstands the 94–96°C denaturation step of PCR. Optimal activity at 72°C. Rate: ~1000 bp/min. Lacks 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease activity.

A programmable device that automatically and precisely controls the temperature cycling of PCR reactions. Alternates between the denaturation, annealing, and extension temperatures for the programmed number of cycles, enabling complete automation of PCR.

The PCR product — the double-stranded DNA fragment amplified between (and including) the two primer sequences. Its size is fixed by the primer positions and is detected as a band on agarose gel electrophoresis.

RNA-dependent DNA polymerase from retroviruses (e.g., MMLV-RT). In RT-PCR, converts single-stranded mRNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) before PCR amplification. Essential for detecting and studying RNA targets including RNA viruses.

protein_databases_app.html.title: Protein Databases: SWISS-PROT, UniProt & PDB
kp: SWISS-PROT: erland / 🇺🇸 USA · SIB & EBI SWISS-PROT — The Manually Curated Protein Sequence Database SWISS-PROT is a manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database that provides high-quality annotation for each entry. It was established in 1986 at the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB) by Amos Bairoch and is now maintained jointly by SIB and the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI) as part of UniProt.
Nucleotide databases (GenBank, EMBL) store DNA/RNA sequences; protein sequence databases (SWISS-PROT, UniProt) store amino acid sequences; structural databases (PDB) store 3D atomic coordinates.
SWISS-PROT: manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database; founded 1986 by Amos Bairoch; maintained by SIB + EBI; now the reviewed tier of UniProt.
UniProt: comprehensive protein resource created 2002; UniProtKB = Swiss-Prot (reviewed, ~570K) + TrEMBL (unreviewed, ~220M entries).
SWISS-PROT is a subset of UniProt — all Swiss-Prot entries are in UniProt, but UniProt contains far more entries.
PDB (Protein Data Bank): world's only archive of 3D macromolecular structures; founded 1971; managed by wwPDB; stores atomic XYZ coordinates, experimental method, ligands.
PDB methods: X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, Cryo-EM. Each structure has a unique 4-character PDB ID (e.g., 1HHO for haemoglobin).
Data flow: lab → database entry → storage → retrieval → analysis/application.
Applications: protein ID (UniProt), functional annotation (Swiss-Prot), drug design (PDB), evolutionary studies (both), disease research (both).
AlphaFold 2 (2021) predicted structures for nearly all human proteins — linking sequence (UniProt) and structure (PDB) databases.

sa.q: What is SWISS-PROT? Describe its features and importance as a protein sequence database.
sa.a: Define SWISS-PROT (manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database; founded 1986 by Amos Bairoch; SIB + EBI; now part of UniProt). Features: manual expert curation, non-redundant entries, rich annotation (sequence, function, PTMs, disease, organism), cross-references to 100+ databases. Importance: gold standard for protein data quality; preferred for reliable biological interpretation; widely cited in molecular biology research.

sa.q: Explain UniProt and its components. What is the relationship between SWISS-PROT and UniProt?
sa.a: UniProt = Universal Protein Resource; created 2002 by SIB + EBI + PIR. Components: UniProtKB (central knowledgebase = Swiss-Prot + TrEMBL), UniRef (sequence clusters), UniParc (archive). Swiss-Prot vs TrEMBL: Swiss-Prot (~570K) = manually reviewed ("gold standard"); TrEMBL (~220M) = computationally annotated, awaiting review. Relationship: SWISS-PROT is a subset (reviewed tier) of UniProt. TrEMBL entries graduate to Swiss-Prot after expert review.

sa.q: What is the Protein Data Bank (PDB)? Describe the type of data it stores and its importance in structural biology.
sa.a: PDB = Protein Data Bank; founded 1971; managed by wwPDB (RCSB, PDBe, PDBj). Data stored: 3D atomic XYZ coordinates (in Å), amino acid/nucleotide sequence, experimental method (X-ray, NMR, Cryo-EM), resolution, ligands, biological assembly. Importance: reveals how proteins fold and function; essential for rational/structure-based drug design; HIV protease inhibitors and COVID-19 antivirals designed using PDB data; training data for AI structure prediction (AlphaFold).

sa.q: Distinguish between protein sequence databases and structural databases. Give two examples of each type.
sa.a: Protein sequence databases: store 1D amino acid sequences + annotations; tell you WHAT the protein is made of; examples: SWISS-PROT, UniProt (UniProtKB). Structural databases: store 3D atomic coordinates; tell you WHAT SHAPE the protein adopts; examples: PDB, AlphaFold Database. Key distinction: a protein can have a known sequence but unknown structure — not all UniProt proteins are in PDB. Structural data requires laborious experimental methods; sequence data is more easily obtained.

sa.q: Discuss the applications of protein and structural databases in biotechnology and drug research.
sa.a: Applications: (1) Protein identification — BLAST search against UniProt/Swiss-Prot; (2) Functional annotation — retrieve known function without lab experiments; (3) Drug design — PDB active site visualisation, molecular docking, virtual screening; (4) Disease research — Swiss-Prot variant annotations; (5) Evolutionary studies — phylogenetic trees from retrieved sequences; (6) Industrial enzymes — search for thermostable or pH-tolerant homologues; (7) Structure prediction validation (AlphaFold vs PDB). Mention specific examples: HIV protease inhibitors, COVID-19 antivirals.

gl.d: The linear order of amino acids in a polypeptide chain (primary structure); determines the protein's identity and, ultimately, its 3D shape and function.
A manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database; the "gold standard" for protein annotation; founded 1986; now the reviewed tier of UniProt.
Universal Protein Resource — the world's most comprehensive protein database, containing UniProtKB (Swiss-Prot + TrEMBL), UniRef, and UniParc; created 2002.
A database in which entries have been manually reviewed and verified by expert scientists — ensuring accuracy but limiting speed and scale.
Biological information added to a sequence or structure entry — protein name, function, subcellular location, post-translational modifications, disease links.
Protein Data Bank — the world's only archive of three-dimensional structures of biological macromolecules; stores atomic XYZ coordinates determined by X-ray, NMR, or Cryo-EM.
The complete spatial arrangement of all atoms in a macromolecule — the tertiary (and quaternary) structure. Stored in PDB as XYZ coordinates in Ångströms.
The branch of molecular biology that studies the molecular structure of biological macromolecules and how structure relates to function.
The biological role a protein performs — enzymatic catalysis, structural support, signalling, transport, or regulation.
The unreviewed tier of UniProtKB — automatically annotated protein sequences from genome sequencing projects; entries await manual curation to graduate to Swiss-Prot.
A unique 4-character alphanumeric identifier assigned to each structure deposited in the Protein Data Bank (e.g., 1HHO for haemoglobin).
Cryo-Electron Microscopy — an experimental technique for determining 3D structures of macromolecules at near-atomic resolution, particularly useful for large complexes.

sanger_dna_sequencing.html.title: DNA Sequencing: Sanger Method
kp: Sanger Method: Developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977 (Nobel Prize 1980). Also called chain-termination or dideoxy method. The gold standard for DNA sequencing.
Key Principle: Uses ddNTPs as chain terminators. ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group → when incorporated, chain synthesis stops permanently.
dNTP vs ddNTP: Only structural difference: dNTP has 3'-OH; ddNTP has 3'-H (no OH). This single difference prevents the next phosphodiester bond formation.
Fragment Ladder: Reaction produces fragments of all possible lengths, each ending at a specific nucleotide type. Reading fragment sizes in order reveals the sequence.
dNTP:ddNTP Ratio: ddNTPs are ~100× more dilute than dNTPs to ensure random incorporation at every position — producing the complete ladder of fragment sizes.
Original Method: Four separate reactions (ddA, ddT, ddG, ddC), radioactive labelling, 4-lane polyacrylamide gel, read bottom to top, autoradiography.
Modern Method: Single reaction, four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (each different colour), capillary electrophoresis, chromatogram output, automated base calling.
Gel Reading: Read bottom to top (smallest = earliest position). Each band's lane/colour = the nucleotide at that position. Sequence is the new strand read 5'→3'.
Read Length & Accuracy: 600–1000 reliable bases per run; >99.99% accuracy for high-quality bases. First 15–40 bases may be unreliable.
Applications: Clone verification, mutation detection, Human Genome Project, clinical diagnostics, pathogen identification, forensics.

Limitation vs NGS: Only ~1 kb per reaction (low throughput); expensive for whole genomes. NGS sequences billions of bases simultaneously but Sanger remains gold standard for accuracy in targeted sequencing.
Correct Step Order: Denature DNA → Anneal primer → Polymerase extends + ddNTP terminates → Fragments of all sizes form → Electrophoresis separates → Read sequence from chromatogram.

sa.q: What is the principle of Sanger's chain termination method of DNA sequencing?
sa.a: Principle: chain-termination (dideoxy method) using dideoxynucleotide triphosphates (ddNTPs) as chain terminators. ddNTPs are structural analogues of normal dNTPs but lack a 3'-OH group (have 3'-H instead). DNA polymerase incorporates ddNTPs into the growing chain at random positions — when ddNTP is incorporated, no further elongation is possible (no 3'-OH for next phosphodiester bond). This produces a population of fragments of all possible lengths, each starting at the primer and ending at a specific base type. Separation by electrophoresis and reading the positions gives the complete sequence. Developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977 (Nobel Prize Chemistry 1980).

sa.q: Why does the incorporation of a dideoxynucleotide (ddNTP) cause chain termination? Explain with reference to its structure.
sa.a: Normal dNTP has: 5'-triphosphate, deoxyribose sugar with 2'-H and 3'-OH, and a nucleobase. ddNTP differs in ONE critical way: the 3' position of the deoxyribose sugar has a hydrogen atom (3'-H) instead of a hydroxyl group (3'-OH). DNA polymerase extends a chain by catalysing an attack of the 3'-OH on the α-phosphate of the incoming dNTP, forming a new 3'–5' phosphodiester bond and releasing pyrophosphate. When a ddNTP is incorporated: its 5'-phosphate forms a bond with the previous nucleotide's 3'-OH. But the ddNTP itself now sits at the 3' end with only a 3'-H — no hydroxyl group is available to attack the next incoming nucleotide. Therefore, no new phosphodiester bond can form → synthesis is permanently halted → chain termination. Include a structural diagram comparing dNTP and ddNTP showing the 3'-OH vs 3'-H difference.

sa.q: Describe the steps involved in Sanger DNA sequencing. How is the sequence determined from the result?
sa.a: Step 1: Denature template DNA to single strands (heat or NaOH). Step 2: Anneal oligonucleotide primer to template (50–60°C). Step 3: Add DNA polymerase, all four dNTPs, and all four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (100× lower concentration than dNTPs). Step 4: Synthesis proceeds; at each position, ddNTP may be randomly incorporated → chain terminates at every possible position → population of fragments of all lengths is produced. Step 5: Fragments denatured and loaded into capillary electrophoresis instrument. Step 6: Fragments separated by size; laser detects fluorescent colour as each fragment elutes. Sequence determination: chromatogram shows coloured peaks; each colour = one base; peaks read left to right (small = earliest in 5'→3' sequence).

sa.q: What is the role of dNTPs and ddNTPs in Sanger sequencing? Why are ddNTPs added at a much lower concentration than dNTPs?
sa.a: Role of dNTPs: Normal building blocks — provide the nucleotide subunits for DNA chain elongation. All four (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP) are needed. Their 3'-OH groups allow the chain to continue growing. Role of ddNTPs: Chain terminators — incorporated randomly at complementary positions and permanently stop synthesis. Each one terminates at a specific base type. In modern sequencing, each carries a different fluorescent dye for base identification. Why low concentration of ddNTPs? If ddNTPs were in equal or higher concentration, almost every fragment would be very short (terminated near the primer). A low ddNTP:dNTP ratio (~1:100) ensures that termination occurs rarely and randomly across the entire length of the template — generating fragments of every possible length from position 1 to ~1000 nt. This complete "ladder" of fragment sizes is essential for reading the full sequence.

sa.q: List the components required for Sanger sequencing. State the advantages and limitations of this method.
sa.a: Components: (1) Template DNA (single-stranded); (2) Primer (specific oligonucleotide); (3) DNA polymerase (Klenow fragment, T7, or Taq); (4) All four dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP); (5) All four ddNTPs (ddATP, ddTTP, ddGTP, ddCTP — each fluorescently labelled); (6) Buffer with Mg²⁺ cofactor. Advantages: High accuracy (>99.99%); long reads (600–1000 bp); gold standard; automated; cost-effective for single genes. Limitations: Low throughput (only ~1 kb per reaction); expensive for whole genomes; first 15–40 bases unreliable; cannot sequence repetitive regions well; requires pure single-sequence template. Brief mention of NGS as higher-throughput alternative, but Sanger remains preferred for targeted, high-accuracy sequencing.

gl.d: The process of determining the precise order of nucleotide bases (A, T, G, C) along a DNA strand. The sequence reveals the genetic information encoded in the DNA molecule.

A DNA sequencing technique developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977, based on the chain-termination principle using dideoxynucleotides. Also called the dideoxy method. Gold standard of DNA sequencing for over 30 years.

A synthetic analogue of a normal deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate (dNTP), lacking a 3'-OH group (replaced by 3'-H). When incorporated by DNA polymerase, it permanently terminates chain elongation. Used as chain terminators in Sanger sequencing.
The permanent halting of DNA synthesis caused by incorporation of a ddNTP. Since ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group, no new phosphodiester bond can be formed — the growing chain cannot be extended further.

The single-stranded DNA molecule used as the blueprint in DNA synthesis. In Sanger sequencing, the template strand is read 3'→5' by DNA polymerase, which synthesises a new complementary strand in the 5'→3' direction.

A short (18–25 nt) synthetic single-stranded oligonucleotide complementary to the template strand. Provides the free 3'-OH required for DNA polymerase to initiate synthesis. Defines the start and direction of sequencing in Sanger method.

A technique that uses an electric field to separate charged molecules (such as DNA fragments) by size. Smaller fragments migrate faster and farther in the gel or capillary. Enables single-nucleotide resolution of Sanger sequencing fragments.

The graphical output of automated fluorescent Sanger sequencing showing coloured peaks on a time axis. Each peak represents one nucleotide — the peak colour identifies the base (A/T/G/C) and peak position reflects fragment size.

A modern, automated separation method used in Sanger sequencing where DNA fragments migrate through a thin polymer-filled capillary tube. Laser detection of fluorescence allows high-resolution, high-throughput sequencing (e.g., ABI 3730xl platform).
Deoxynucleoside triphosphate — the normal building block of DNA. Contains a deoxyribose sugar with a free 3'-OH group that allows continued chain elongation. Four types: dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP.

screening_selection_recombinants.html.title: Screening & Selection of Recombinants
kp: Need for Screening: After transformation, all colony types look identical. Selection/screening is essential to identify cells with the correct recombinant vector among transformed and non-transformed cells.
Selection vs Screening: Selection = cells either survive or die (antibiotic). Screening = all cells survive but a signal distinguishes recombinants (colour, probe signal).
Direct Selection: Antibiotic resistance on vector. Only transformants survive. Does NOT distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant. FIRST step always.
Insertional Inactivation: pBR322 example. Insert into BamHI site disrupts tet^r. Recombinants: amp^r, tet^s. Identified by replica plating. Recombinants absent from tet plate.
Blue-White Selection: pUC19 vector. Insert in MCS disrupts lacZ-α. Blue = non-recombinant (lacZ intact, X-gal cleaved). White = recombinant (lacZ disrupted). Needs X-gal + IPTG in medium.
Colony Hybridization: Most specific method. Labelled probe hybridises to target gene. Steps: colony blot → lysis (NaOH) → DNA fixation → probe → wash → autoradiograph → pick from master plate.
X-gal: Colourless β-galactosidase substrate. Cleaved by intact β-gal → blue compound. NOT an antibiotic — a chromogenic substrate.
IPTG: Non-hydrolysable lac operon inducer. Ensures lacZ-α is expressed for blue-white screening. NOT an antibiotic — a transcriptional inducer.
pBR322 vs pUC19: pBR322 → insertional inactivation (two antibiotic genes: amp^r + tet^r). pUC19 → blue-white selection (lacZ-α + MCS). Both also used with direct antibiotic selection.
Probe in Colony Hybridization: ³²P-labelled ssDNA or RNA. Complementary to gene of interest. After hybridisation and washing, positive colonies detected by autoradiography on X-ray film.

α-Complementation: In blue-white, the vector supplies lacZ-α fragment and the host (DH5α, JM109) supplies lacZ-ω. Together they form active β-galactosidase. Insert disrupts α-peptide → no complementation → white colony.

Correct Workflow Order: Transform → plate on antibiotic (direct selection) → screen for recombinant (blue-white or insertional inactivation) → confirm with colony hybridization or PCR → verify by sequencing.

sa.q: What is the difference between selection and screening in the context of gene cloning? Give one example of each.
sa.a: Selection: An active process where only cells with the desired property survive on selective medium; non-selected cells are eliminated. Example: plating transformed E. coli on ampicillin — only cells with the vector (carrying amp^r gene) survive; non-transformed cells die. Screening: A passive process where all cells survive, but a detectable signal (colour, probe signal) allows identification of cells with the desired property without killing others. Example: blue-white screening — all transformants survive, but recombinants form white colonies while non-recombinants form blue colonies. Key difference: selection = growth/no growth; screening = identifying among surviving colonies. Selection is always step 1 (reduces to transformants); screening is step 2 (identifies recombinants among transformants).

sa.q: Describe insertional inactivation using pBR322. How are recombinant clones identified?
sa.a: pBR322 has two antibiotic resistance genes: amp^r and tet^r. The tet^r gene contains unique restriction sites BamHI, SalI, and ClaI. When the gene of interest is cloned into the BamHI site (within tet^r), the tet^r gene is disrupted → recombinant cells become tetracycline-sensitive. After transformation, cells are plated on LB + ampicillin → all transformants (both recombinant and non-recombinant) grow. Replica plating to LB + tetracycline: non-recombinants (intact tet^r) grow on both plates; recombinants (disrupted tet^r) grow only on amp plate — ABSENT on tet plate. Recombinants identified as colonies present on amp plate but absent on tet plate. These are picked from the original amp master plate. Result: amp^r, tet^s = recombinant. amp^r, tet^r = non-recombinant.

sa.q: Explain blue-white selection. Why are white colonies considered recombinants in this system?
sa.a: Blue-white selection uses pUC vectors (e.g., pUC19) that carry the lacZ-α gene with the MCS inserted within it. Medium: LB + ampicillin (to select transformants) + X-gal (chromogenic substrate for β-gal) + IPTG (lac operon inducer). Without insert: lacZ-α is intact → IPTG induces expression → functional β-galactosidase α-peptide produced (by α-complementation with host lacZ-ω) → β-gal cleaves X-gal → blue compound → BLUE colony = non-recombinant. With insert in MCS: lacZ-α reading frame is disrupted → no functional α-peptide → no α-complementation → β-gal cannot cleave X-gal → no blue compound → colony remains WHITE = recombinant. Therefore, white colonies have an insert disrupting lacZ → they are recombinant transformants. White ≠ necessarily has the correct insert — further confirmation needed (PCR, restriction analysis, sequencing).

sa.q: Describe the steps involved in colony hybridization for identifying recombinant colonies.
sa.a: 1. Colony transfer: Replica nylon/nitrocellulose membrane placed on master plate — colonies adhere; membrane peeled off. Keep master plate as reference. 2. Cell lysis: Membrane treated with NaOH — cells lyse, DNA released and denatured into single strands. 3. DNA fixation: Membrane baked at 80°C (2 hrs) or UV-cross-linked — single-stranded DNA permanently immobilised on membrane. 4. Pre-hybridisation (blocking): Non-specific sites blocked with salmon sperm DNA/BSA to reduce background. 5. Probe hybridisation: ³²P-labelled ssDNA probe (complementary to gene of interest) added. Probe anneals only to complementary target sequences at appropriate stringency. 6. Washing: Non-specifically bound probe washed off with increasing stringency washes. 7. Detection: Membrane exposed to X-ray film (autoradiography) — positive colonies appear as dark spots. 8. Identification: Alignment marks used to match positive spots on film to corresponding colonies on master plate. Positive colonies picked for further analysis.

sa.q: Compare insertional inactivation and blue-white selection as methods of screening recombinants. Which is more convenient and why?
sa.a: Insertional Inactivation: Vector pBR322. Insert disrupts tet^r at BamHI site. Recombinants: amp^r, tet^s. Identified by REPLICA PLATING (negative result — absent from tet plate). Two plates needed. Takes 2 days. No special reagents. Blue-White Selection: Vector pUC19. Insert disrupts lacZ-α at MCS. Recombinants: white colonies. Non-recombinants: blue colonies. Identified on SAME plate (positive visual result). One plate, one step. Requires X-gal + IPTG. Blue-white is more convenient because: (a) results visible on the same plate without replica plating; (b) positive visual identification (white = recombinant) vs negative identification (absent from tet plate); (c) faster (overnight); (d) less technically demanding. Both are used after direct antibiotic selection; neither confirms the CORRECT insert — only that some insert is present. Colony hybridization is still needed to confirm the specific gene.

gl.d: A cell or organism containing foreign DNA that has been introduced into its genome or as an episomal element. In gene cloning, a recombinant clone is a bacterial colony carrying a vector with the gene of interest inserted into its MCS.

A gene (typically an antibiotic resistance gene) on a cloning vector used to identify transformed host cells. Only cells expressing the marker gene survive on selective medium. Examples: amp^r, kan^r, tet^r, neo^r.

The disruption of a marker gene's function by inserting foreign DNA into a restriction site within it. Used to distinguish recombinant (marker-inactive) from non-recombinant (marker-active) transformants. Classic example: pBR322 tet^r disrupted by insert at BamHI site.

The E. coli gene encoding β-galactosidase. In pUC vectors, the lacZ-α fragment (with MCS within it) is used for blue-white screening. An insert in the MCS disrupts lacZ-α → no functional β-galactosidase → colony remains white (recombinant).

5-Bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-β-D-galactopyranoside. A colourless chromogenic substrate for β-galactosidase. Cleavage by active β-gal releases a blue insoluble compound (5-bromo-4-chloro-indigo), producing blue colonies in blue-white screening.

Isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside. A non-metabolisable inducer of the E. coli lac operon. Induces expression of lacZ-α in pUC vectors during blue-white screening, ensuring sufficient β-galactosidase production for a visible blue signal.

A labelled single-stranded DNA or RNA molecule complementary to a specific target sequence. Used in colony hybridization to identify colonies containing the gene of interest by sequence-specific base pairing. Labelled with ³²P, digoxigenin, or biotin.

A molecular screening technique where bacterial colonies are transferred to a membrane, lysed, DNA denatured and fixed, and then probed with a labelled nucleic acid probe. Positive colonies (hybridised to probe) are detected by autoradiography and picked from the master plate.

A technique for making an exact copy of colony positions from one plate to another, using a sterile velvet pad. Used in insertional inactivation to compare growth on ampicillin vs tetracycline plates to identify recombinants (absent on tet plate = amp^r, tet^s).

The reconstitution of functional β-galactosidase by combining the lacZ-α peptide (from pUC vector) with the lacZ-ω peptide (from host strain). An insert in the MCS disrupts lacZ-α → no complementation → no functional β-gal → white colony (recombinant).

animal_cell_culture.html.title: Animal Cell Culture Techniques
kp: Animal cell culture: growth of cells isolated from animal tissue in vitro under controlled temperature (37 °C), pH (7.2–7.4), CO₂ (5–10%) and nutrition.
Milestones: Harrison 1907 (nerve fibre culture); Earle 1943 (mouse fibroblast line); HeLa 1951 (first immortal human line); hybridoma 1975; human ES cells 1998; iPSC 2006 (Yamanaka).

Sterilisation: autoclave 121 °C, 15 psi, 15–20 min (media, glassware); dry heat 160–170 °C (glassware); 0.22 µm filtration for serum and heat-labile media; 70% ethanol for surfaces; UV 254 nm in the cabinet.
pH is monitored with phenol red (yellow = acidic) and buffered by bicarbonate (with CO₂) or HEPES; osmolarity 280–320 mOsm/kg.
Media: natural (plasma, serum, tissue extracts, embryo extract) and synthetic (DMEM, RPMI 1640, MEM, Ham’s F12); serum-free and protein-free media remove batch variability and contamination risk.
Primary culture: cells taken directly from tissue (mechanical or enzymatic dissociation with trypsin or collagenase); finite life span, heterogeneous; explant versus monolayer.
Trypan blue exclusion: live cells stay clear, dead cells stain blue; viability should be ≥ 90% before seeding.
Subculture (passage) of adherent cells: PBS wash, trypsin-EDTA, neutralise with serum medium, split 1:3 to 1:10; normal cells are finite (Hayflick limit, ~50 divisions).
Continuous lines: HeLa (cervical carcinoma), CHO (hamster ovary, biopharmaceuticals), Vero (monkey kidney, vaccines), NIH 3T3, MCF-7, Jurkat, PC12.
Cryopreservation: ~10% DMSO, cool at −1 °C/min, store in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C; thaw rapidly at 37 °C and dilute the DMSO.
Stem cells: ESC (pluripotent, from inner cell mass), iPSC (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc), HSC (CD34⁺, bone-marrow transplant), MSC (osteoblasts, chondrocytes, adipocytes), NSC (neurospheres).
Organ culture preserves 3-D architecture: watch-glass (Fell and Robison), grid/raft, perfusion and roller-tube methods.
Artificial skin: keratinocytes + fibroblasts on a collagen scaffold, air–liquid interface for stratification; Apligraf, Integra, Epicel, Dermagraft; limits: no vessels, nerves or glands.

sa.q: Define animal cell culture and mention its applications.
sa.a: Growth of cells removed from an animal in vitro under controlled temperature, pH, CO₂ and nutrition. Applications: vaccine and biopharmaceutical production, cancer biology, drug screening, genetic engineering, tissue engineering and virology.

sa.q: List the basic requirements for animal cell culture.
sa.a: Physical: 37 °C, pH 7.2–7.4, 5–10% CO₂, ≥95% humidity. Chemical: basal medium (DMEM/RPMI) with serum or defined supplements. Biological: correct inoculum density and timely subculture. Sterility: biosafety cabinet, antibiotics, aseptic technique.

sa.q: Differentiate natural and synthetic media.
sa.a: Natural media are biological fluids (plasma, serum, tissue extracts, embryo extract); they are rich but variable. Synthetic media are chemically defined (DMEM, RPMI 1640, MEM, Ham’s F12), usually with 10% serum, or serum-free and protein-free versions.

sa.q: Describe the establishment of a primary culture.
sa.a: Collect tissue aseptically, wash in PBS, mince, dissociate with trypsin or collagenase, filter, centrifuge at 200 × g, resuspend in complete medium, count with a haemocytometer and trypan blue (viability ≥ 90%), seed and incubate at 37 °C with 5% CO₂.

sa.q: How are cell lines subcultured and preserved?
sa.a: At 80–90% confluence: wash with PBS, add trypsin-EDTA, neutralise with serum medium, centrifuge, resuspend and split 1:3 to 1:10. For storage: freeze in medium with 10% DMSO at −1 °C/min and keep at −196 °C.

sa.q: Compare finite and continuous cell lines.
sa.a: Finite lines have a limited life span (~20–50 passages, Hayflick limit) and retain normal diploid features. Continuous lines (HeLa, CHO, Vero) are immortal, often aneuploid and transformed.

sa.q: Write short notes on ESCs and iPSCs.
sa.a: ESCs come from the blastocyst inner cell mass and are pluripotent; cultured on MEF feeders or Matrigel with LIF (mouse) or bFGF (human). iPSCs are somatic cells reprogrammed with Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc (Yamanaka 2006), avoiding embryo use and allowing autologous therapy.

sa.q: Explain organ culture and name its methods.
sa.a: Organ culture maintains whole organs or fragments in vitro with their 3-D structure. Methods: watch-glass/plasma clot, grid or raft at the liquid–air interface, perfusion and roller-tube.

sa.q: Describe the production of artificial skin.
sa.a: Keratinocytes from a patient biopsy are expanded; fibroblasts are seeded in a collagen dermal scaffold; keratinocytes are placed on top and cultured at an air–liquid interface for 14–21 days to stratify and cornify; quality is tested before grafting onto burns or ulcers.

gl.d: Outside the living organism, for example in a culture flask.
Culture started directly from tissue; finite and heterogeneous.
Culture derived by subculturing a primary culture; finite or continuous.
Percentage of the growth surface covered by adherent cells.
Transfer of cells to fresh medium and vessels (subculture).
Protease that detaches adherent cells by cleaving surface proteins.
pH indicator in medium: yellow when acidic, pink-red at neutral, purple when alkaline.
Fetal bovine serum; supplies growth factors, hormones and attachment proteins.
Finite number (~50) of divisions of normal somatic cells.
Storage of cells at −196 °C in liquid nitrogen with a cryoprotectant such as DMSO.
Able to form all three germ layers.
Inactivated cells (for example MEFs) that support growth of stem cells.
Three-dimensional miniature organ-like structure grown from stem cells.
